name: Keeping Seniors on Track Over the Summer
title: Keeping Seniors on Track Over the Summer
answer: Summer melt is the loss of college-bound students between graduation and enrollment, and it falls hardest on those with the least support at home. Keeping in touch with seniors over the summer through personalized messages and peer or staff outreach helps them complete tasks like deposits, transcripts, and orientation. The support matters most for first generation students, who often have no one at home who has been through the process.

sections.body: Summer melt describes what happens when students who intend to go to college never actually enroll, and it hits hardest among students with the least support. Once graduation passes, students lose contact with their counselors right when they face practical tasks such as paying deposits, sending final transcripts, and signing up for orientation. Without someone to remind them and answer quick questions, some simply give up. The idea is to keep a line of contact open through the summer so those small tasks do not become the reason a student never shows up. It solves a gap in the system rather than a gap in the student.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: Schools can use texting platforms to stay in touch with seniors across the summer months. A counselor or another staff member should monitor the replies and answer the questions the tool cannot handle. The outreach should stop once a student has enrolled or has chosen a different path. Families should be told that the outreach is happening and how to opt out. The text does not give separate grade band guidance, since the practice concerns graduating seniors.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels this idea with research behind it. An early trial found that personalized text messages and outreach from peer mentors over the summer raised college enrollment, especially for students with less access to counseling (Castleman & Page, 2015). The chatbot trial described at the start of the chapter found similar effects with an AI tool (Page & Gehlbach, 2017). A later trial with 4,442 admitted students found that chatbot outreach helped most with financial aid steps, and that the benefits were concentrated among first generation college students (Nurshatayeva et al., 2021).
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text sets clear limits on how this outreach should run. A person, not the tool, stays responsible for monitoring replies and answering what the tool cannot. The messages should end once students have enrolled or chosen another path, so the contact does not continue past its purpose. Families should know the outreach is happening and should be given a way to opt out. The decisions about a student's next step remain with the student and family, and the reminders exist only to support them.
